articles.title: Agentes de IA que nunca saem do navegador
articles.excerpt: Você já se cansou de copiar e colar dados entre tabs porque sua ferramenta de IA A maioria dos agentes de IA hoje funciona assim: você descreve o que quer, WebMCP (Model Context Protocol para a Web) v…
articles.body: Você já se cansou de copiar e colar dados entre tabs porque sua ferramenta de IA não consegue "ver" o sistema que você está usando? WebMCP resolve isso deixando sites exporem ferramentas que agentes podem chamar — sem sair do browser, sem mandar seus dados pra nuvem. Por que isso importa agora A maioria dos agentes de IA hoje funciona assim: você descreve o que quer, o agente manda o pedido pra um servidor na nuvem, processa, e te devolve uma resposta genérica. Se o agente precisa interagir com um app web que você está usando, ele não consegue — a menos que você exponha uma API pública ou construa integrações customizadas.
articles.author: Taina Costa

articles.title: See which bots and AI crawlers are visiting your Angular site
articles.excerpt: If a crawler downloads a page without running JavaScript, an Angular service or HTTP interceptor will never see it. The request still reaches the server that delivers your site. This walkthrough puts…
articles.body: If a crawler downloads a page without running JavaScript, an Angular service or HTTP interceptor will never see it. The request still reaches the server that delivers your site. This walkthrough puts WebDecoy in front of Angular's server-side rendering handler. You can observe requests in monitor mode, inspect the results, and keep serving the application while you decide what needs a response. We build WebDecoy. This tutorial was prepared with AI assistance and uses a runnable example from our public SDK repository. It covers WebDecoy request detection, not FCaptcha.

articles.title: Don't Block Your GPU: Architecting a Distributed AI Audio Backend with FastAPI, Celery, and Redis
articles.excerpt: 1. The Event Loop Trap (Why Your API is Crashing) You’ve just built a brilliant AI audio transcription system using PyTorch and Faster-Whisper. It works flawlessly in your local environment. To show i…
articles.body: 1. The Event Loop Trap (Why Your API is Crashing) You’ve just built a brilliant AI audio transcription system using PyTorch and Faster-Whisper. It works flawlessly in your local environment. To show it to the world, you wrap it in a FastAPI endpoint, deploy it, and send a test request. It works perfectly. Then, three users upload audio files at the exact same time. Suddenly, your server freezes, new requests time out, and your terminal spits out the dreaded RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory What just happened? Welcome to the Event Loop Trap . Here is the exact anti-pattern that causes this nightmare: @app.post ( " /transcribe " ) async def transcribe_audio ( file : UploadFile ): # THE TRAP: This synchronous, compute-bound task blocks the entire event loop! result = whisper_model .

articles.title: How the Web Actually Works: A Developer's Mental Model of Modern Architecture
articles.excerpt: I spent a long time writing code before I genuinely understood what happened after I hit Enter on a URL. I knew about frontend and backend. I had a vague sense that CDNs existed. But if someone asked…
articles.body: I spent a long time writing code before I genuinely understood what happened after I hit Enter on a URL. I knew about frontend and backend. I had a vague sense that CDNs existed. But if someone asked me to draw the path a request takes from a browser to a database and back — I would have drawn something embarrassingly incomplete. This post is the explanation I wish I had early on. No Docker. No Kubernetes deep-dives. Just the foundational mental model of how modern web architecture actually fits together — the pieces every developer should be able to reason about clearly. What Actually Happens When You Type a URL Let us start with the most fundamental question: you open a browser, type https://example.com , and press Enter. What happens?

articles.title: A Learning Platform Run By Agents
articles.excerpt: The most interesting part of our learning platform is not the content. It is the question of who makes it. The Academy is a site with lessons, recipes and guides for building your own AI systems, in s…
articles.body: The most interesting part of our learning platform is not the content. It is the question of who makes it. The Academy is a site with lessons, recipes and guides for building your own AI systems, in six levels from the entry point to your own MCP server. It has no editorial team in the usual sense. It has a group of agents, each with a role. The Roles There is one that researches what is moving out there. One that turns that into topic proposals. One that writes. One that reviews what was written and is allowed to reject it. One that watches the numbers, meaning what gets read and what sits idle. And one that checks whether the site appears in AI answers at all. That division is the actual trick. An agent reviewing its own text finds nothing.

articles.title: Your next Google Play subscription could work very differently
articles.excerpt: New tools also add bundles, team seats, and smarter payment recovery.
articles.body: TL;DR Google Play is adding usage-based subscription billing aimed at AI apps and other services with variable costs. New options will also support team subscriptions, mixed subscription/one-time purchases, and cross-app bundles. Google is also testing smarter grace periods, cancellation discounts, cheaper-plan offers, and Play Store winback deals. Google Play’s billing story changed earlier this year when Google opened the door wider to alternative billing systems and external web payments, giving Android users more choice over how they pay. Now it is turning its attention to subscriptions that still run through Google Play itself, with new billing options that could make AI apps, bundles, and failed payments work very differently for users.

articles.title: The US government now has an AI chatbot, and Google is helping power it
articles.excerpt: Bringing over 29,000 official government sources under one roof.
articles.body: TL;DR America.gov is a new AI-powered US government portal that pulls information from more than 29,000 official sources. The Google-backed platform can answer questions about benefits, forms, fees, deadlines, and eligibility, while also supporting PDF uploads and voice input. America.gov is limited to providing information at launch, but it plans to support forms, applications, and renewals starting in 2027. There’s no shortage of information about all the federal services and critical public resources available to Americans, but parsing through sources to actually find the right info when you need it can be a headache. The US government seems to know that, and it is now leveraging Google’s AI to bring all important federal information and services under one roof.

articles.title: NASA Opens Applications for Second Season of ORBIT Student Challenge
articles.excerpt: Following a successful inaugural year of ingenuity and career building, NASA ORBIT (Opportunities in Research, Business, Innovation, and Technology) has officially returned for a second season to brin…
articles.body: 2 Min Read NASA Opens Applications for Second Season of ORBIT Student Challenge Following a successful inaugural year of ingenuity and career building, NASA ORBIT (Opportunities in Research, Business, Innovation, and Technology) has officially returned for a second season to bring university and college student innovation to the forefront of Earth technology development and deep-space exploration. Registration for the 2026–2027 challenge is open through Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, through the NASA STEM Gateway . Expanded for its second season with up to $500,000 in total prize funding, NASA’s ORBIT invites student teams to explore their boldest ideas and invent their brightest solutions.

articles.title: Under the Microscope: NASA-Made Material for Moon Manufacturing
articles.excerpt: Photos taken using a microscope reveal the colorful, kaleidoscope-like crystal structure of a new NASA-made material that could be used for manufacturing during future space missions. Developed at NAS…
articles.body: Credit: NASA Credit: NASA Photos taken using a microscope reveal the colorful, kaleidoscope-like crystal structure of a new NASA-made material that could be used for manufacturing during future space missions. Developed at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, the material could be created directly on the Moon or Mars, allowing NASA to pack fewer supplies — saving weight and reducing launch costs.  To make the material, research chemical engineer Allison Christy and her team of summer interns at NASA Glenn — Tyler Klinchuch, Ethan Bilodeau, and Emma Levenson — mixed a special plastic with simulated Moon and Mars dust.
